name: SSRIs for BDD

lead: SSRIs are antidepressants also used for obsessive-compulsive spectrum conditions, including body dysmorphic disorder. In BDD the payoff is fewer obsessive thoughts about a perceived flaw and a calmer, more confident self-view. They are a medical treatment prescribed by clinicians, not an appearance product.

They block reuptake of serotonin, raising its availability between nerve cells, and with continued use the brain adapts in ways thought to relate to their effects. They are among the medications used for BDD and are often combined with CBT. They have been studied for BDD symptoms, not for looks.

paras: A clinician prescribes them as part of a treatment plan, often alongside CBT. Effects build gradually over weeks rather than at once, and treatment is monitored by the prescriber.

Common class effects include sexual side effects and emotional blunting. Stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms. An FDA boxed warning advises monitoring people under 25 for suicidal thoughts. They are prescription-only and used under medical supervision.

trials.title: CBT as an Adjunct to SRIs in the Treatment of BDD

angle.text: SSRIs are prescribed for BDD to ease obsessive preoccupation with a perceived flaw, which leaves people calmer and more confident in how they see themselves. They are mentioned in looksmaxxing forums in that context and are studied for BDD symptoms as a medical treatment.

lead: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are antidepressants that block the serotonin transporter, increasing serotonin availability in the synapse.[1] They are among the medications used in treating body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), a condition involving preoccupation with a perceived flaw in appearance. Wikipedia's BDD article describes SSRIs and cognitive-behavioral therapy as effective treatments, and suggests SSRIs may ease obsessive-compulsive and delusional features.[2]
They are prescription medications used under medical supervision. This article covers general information only, not dosing.

paras: BDD is classified in the obsessive-compulsive spectrum in the DSM-5, and SSRIs are used in it as they are in obsessive-compulsive disorder.[2][1] In OCD, Wikipedia reports that SSRIs are first-line in some national guidelines and that, in children and adolescents, combining them with exposure therapy is probably more effective than an SSRI alone.[1]
A registered phase 4 trial, 'CBT as an Adjunct to SRIs in the Treatment of BDD', started in 2008 with 17 participants and was terminated.[3]

Reported effects of the SSRI class include sexual dysfunction, emotional blunting, bleeding risk, akathisia, and, rarely, serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic drugs.[1] Stopping abruptly can cause discontinuation symptoms.[1]

The FDA's boxed warning advises close monitoring of people under 25 for increased suicidal thoughts and behavior, concentrated in the first one to two months of treatment, according to Wikipedia's summary.[1]

The only trial record in the source set is the terminated phase 4 study of cognitive-behavioral therapy added to serotonin reuptake inhibitors in BDD, which enrolled 17 people.[3] Larger trial results on SSRIs for BDD are not summarized here.
